args.body:
DEAL TEAM REPORT — CHANGE OF CONTROL AND ASSIGNMENT PROVISIONS
Corporate M&A — Analysis of Change of Control Provisions Across Target's Material Contracts

Prepared for: Deal Team / Transaction Committee
Matter: Corporate M&A — Analyze Change of Control Provisions Across Target's Material Contracts (Due Diligence Report)
Deliverable: coc-analysis-report.docx

--------------------------------------------------------------------
I. SCOPE AND PURPOSE
--------------------------------------------------------------------
This report reviews the acquisition data room contracts and the internal memo for change of control ("CoC") and assignment provisions, and reconciles the counterparty's latest markup against the base materials. It identifies every deviation introduced in the counterparty markup, assesses each against the operative agreement, the governing disclosure schedules and exhibits, and market/firm precedent, and provides a recommendation for each.

The analysis is grounded in three operative sources:
  (1) the base materials (the operative agreement containing representations and warranties, covenants, conditions to closing, indemnification, and termination provisions);
  (2) the disclosure schedules and exhibits qualifying the base materials (Schedules 3.7 and 5.2 and Exhibit B); and
  (3) the counterparty markup.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
II. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
--------------------------------------------------------------------
The counterparty's revision accepts the majority of the firm-standard provisions but introduces three material deviations. Each deviation must be reconciled against the base materials and the controlling disclosures:

  1. INDEMNIFICATION: The indemnification cap is silently reduced, and the basket is converted from a deductible to a tipping (threshold) basket.
  2. MATERIAL ADVERSE EFFECT (MAE): The definition of MAE adds carve-outs for regulatory action of exactly the kind at issue in this matter (the two pending regulatory inquiries disclosed on Schedule 3.7).
  3. SURVIVAL PERIOD: A new limitation period shortens the survival of the core representations, contradicting the survival matrix set out in Exhibit B.

Moreover, the markup implicates the treatment of retained liabilities disclosed on Schedule 5.2, which the indemnification changes would silently shift to the buyer unless expressly preserved.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
III. DEVIATION-BY-DEVIATION RECONCILIATION
--------------------------------------------------------------------

DEVIATION 1 — Indemnification cap silently reduced; basket converted from deductible to tipping basket

Base materials / governing source:
The operative agreement (base materials) contains indemnification provisions negotiated between the parties, including an indemnification cap and a deductible-based basket. Firm/market-standard treatment contemplates (a) a stated indemnification cap and (b) a deductible (a "first-dollar" basket whereby the indemnitee bears claims up to the threshold before recovering, on a dollar-for-dollar basis above it).

Counterparty markup deviation:
The counterparty "silently reduces" the indemnification cap and converts the basket from a deductible to a tipping basket (a threshold below which no recovery is available, but above which the full amount of claims — including amounts below the threshold — is recoverable).

Qualifying disclosures:
Schedule 5.2 lists retained liabilities. These retained liabilities are carved out of the seller's indemnification obligations. Under the markup, reducing the cap and switching to a tipping basket would increase the seller's effective recovery threshold and, combined with the Schedule 5.2 retained-liability carve-outs, would silently shift a greater share of liability risk to the buyer.

Assessment:
Two distinct risks are presented. First, the silent reduction of the indemnification cap erodes the buyer's aggregate protection and is a direct, adverse change that must be corrected to the agreed cap. Second, the deductible-to-tipping conversion is a structural change that increases the effective threshold for recovery and is value-shifting. Both changes were introduced without express disclosure, and neither is consistent with the negotiated base position.

Recommendation:
Reject the silent cap reduction and restore the negotiated indemnification cap from the base materials. With respect to the basket, the client's controlling position is to CONCEDE the conversion of the basket from a deductible to a tipping basket. This is a concession the client is prepared to accept. Accordingly, we recommend accepting the basket conversion to a tipping basket, subject to ensuring the tipped amount is applied consistently and that the Schedule 5.2 retained-liability carve-outs remain unchanged. The cap reduction, however, must be rejected and the base cap reinstated.

DEVIATION 2 — MAE definition adds carve-outs for regulatory action

Governing source / disclosures:
Schedule 3.7 discloses two pending regulatory inquiries. The base materials' MAE definition did not carve out regulatory actions of the kind at issue. Market-standard MAE carve-outs typically exclude general economic, financial, and industry conditions, but materially adverse effects caused by regulatory action directed at the target were not carved out in the base materials.

Counterparty markup deviation:
The markup adds carve-outs to the MAE definition for "regulatory action of exactly the kind at issue in this matter" — i.e., carve-outs that would exclude from the definition of MAE the adverse effects arising from the two pending regulatory inquiries disclosed on Schedule 3.7.

Assessment:
This is a materially adverse, deal-protective change for the seller and value-eroding for the buyer. By carving out the very regulatory inquiries currently pending against the target, the markup would permit the seller to omit those effects from the MAE determination, weakening the buyer's ability to invoke MAE-based termination or closing conditions if those inquiries mature into adverse outcomes. Because Schedule 3.7 specifically discloses two pending regulatory inquiries, the proposed carve-out is directly targeted at a live, known risk, not a general market exception.

Recommendation:
REJECT this deviation. The carve-outs for regulatory action of the kind at issue are not supported by the base materials, would undermine the buyer's MAE protection as to known risks, and contradict the disclosure posture reflected in Schedule 3.7. The MAE definition should be restored to the base-market version without the targeted regulatory carve-outs, or, at most, recast so that any regulatory carve-out does not exclude effects arising from the two disclosed pending inquiries.

DEVIATION 3 — New limitation period shortens survival for core representations

Governing source / disclosures:
Exhibit B sets the survival matrix for the representations and warranties, establishing the periods during which each category of representation survives closing. The base materials reflect those survival periods as negotiated.

Counterparty markup deviation:
The markup introduces a new limitation period that shortens the survival period for the core representations, contradicting the survival matrix in Exhibit B. Under Delaware M&A practice, the survival period is a fundamental allocation of post-closing risk; shortening the survival of core (fundamental) representations reduces the window in which the buyer may bring indemnity claims for breaches.

Assessment:
This deviation is squarely inconsistent with Exhibit B, which sets the survival periods the parties agreed. Because the schedules and exhibits control over general statements in the base materials, the markup's shorter period directly conflicts with the operative survival matrix and cannot stand on the current record.

Recommendation:
REJECT this deviation. Restore the survival periods for the core representations to those set out in Exhibit B. Any reduction in the survival period is treated by the client as a walk-away issue. Insist on the Exhibit B survival matrix and decline the shorter limitation period.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
IV. RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN THE DEVIATIONS AND THE DISCLOSURE SCHEDULES
--------------------------------------------------------------------
The schedules and exhibits qualify the base materials and control over general statements in them. Three intersections are material:

  - Schedule 3.7 (pending regulatory inquiries): Directly intersects Deviation 2. The markup's proposed regulatory-action carve-out is targeted at the exact pending inquiries disclosed on Schedule 3.7. Any MAE carve-out that would exclude the effect of those inquiries materially weakens the buyer's position and must be rejected.

  - Schedule 5.2 (retained liabilities): Directly intersects Deviation 1. The retained liabilities disclosed on Schedule 5.2 are carved out of the seller's indemnification. Reducing the cap and converting the basket to a tipping basket would silently expand the portion of liability the buyer bears, in tension with the intended retained-liability allocation. The cap/basket and retained-liability treatment must be read together, and the markup must not shift Schedule 5.2 liabilities to the buyer.

  - Exhibit B (survival matrix): Directly intersects Deviation 3. Exhibit B controls the survival periods. The markup's shorter limitation period contradicts Exhibit B and must be rejected so that the survival matrix governs.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
V. SUMMARY OF RECOMMENDATIONS
--------------------------------------------------------------------
| # | Deviation | Recommendation |
|---|-----------|----------------|
| 1 | Indemnification cap reduced; basket converted to tipping basket | Reject cap reduction (restore base cap); CONCEDE basket conversion to tipping basket |
| 2 | MAE adds regulatory-action carve-outs (Schedule 3.7) | REJECT — restore base MAE definition; do not exclude disclosed pending inquiries |
| 3 | Limitation period shortens survival of core reps (Exhibit B) | REJECT — restore Exhibit B survival matrix; any survival reduction is a walk-away issue |

--------------------------------------------------------------------
VI. RISKS AND FOLLOW-UP ITEMS
--------------------------------------------------------------------
- Confirm the base indemnification cap amount and ensure it is reinstated in the markup.
- Confirm the agreed tipping threshold for the basket if the conversion is conceded, and confirm consistency of the Schedule 5.2 retained-liability treatment.
- Confirm with the regulatory team the status and potential exposure of the two pending regulatory inquiries on Schedule 3.7 to evaluate the adequacy of MAE protection.
- Confirm the survival matrix in Exhibit B is the operative, post-markup version and that the limitation-period change is removed.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
VII. GOVERNING-LAW / PRACTICE NOTE
--------------------------------------------------------------------
The analysis is grounded in Delaware M&A market practice, under which indemnification caps, baskets (deductibles versus tipping), MAE carve-outs, and survival periods are negotiated allocations of post-closing risk. Disclosure schedules and exhibits control over general statements in the operative agreement. Any deviation from the base provisions, absent agreement, must be identified and reconciled before execution.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
DISCLAIMER: This report is prepared for discussion among the deal team and is based solely on the base materials, the disclosure schedules and exhibits, and the counterparty markup described above. It does not constitute a legal opinion.
